approachQuestion.prompt:
Repeated registry checks

An immutable unsorted array contains n distinct integer registry keys. You must answer q membership queries offline, returning one Boolean per query. n>=2, q>=1. Hashing is unavailable. Use comparison-based methods, minimize worst-case total work for arbitrary q by choosing between direct scanning and a sorted-index strategy; break equal asymptotic totals by memory. Example: keys=[8,2,5], queries=[5,7,2] -> [true,false,true]. Inputs cannot be modified.
constraints: Use only the stated input ordering and access guarantees.

options.text: Compare the costs of scanning each query versus copying keys once, comparison-sorting the copy, and binary-searching all queries; choose the cheaper strategy for n and q.
options.feedback: Preprocessing is worthwhile only when enough future queries repay its cost; immutable input makes the sorted copy an explicit space cost.

options.text: Always copy and comparison-sort the keys once, then binary-search all queries, regardless of q.
options.feedback: This is correct, but for q=1 a scan avoids unnecessary sorting. Choosing based on q removes that cost.

options.text: Binary-search the supplied unsorted keys directly for every query.
options.feedback: For keys=[8,2,5], query=8, ordinary binary search can discard index 0 and miss the key.

Preprocessing is worthwhile only when enough future queries repay its cost; immutable input makes the sorted copy an explicit space cost.

Sorting pays a preparation cost to reduce each later membership query. For few queries, scanning avoids that preparation and the copied buffer. Choose using both n and q; sorted lookup is not automatically better for every workload.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For target-method, choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Analyze the adaptive method with a worst-case O(n log n) comparison sort on a copied buffer using at most O(n) work space. Input keys and q output Booleans are excluded; scanning uses scalar memory. q and n may both vary; comparisons and copying one key are constant time. Input storage and returned result storage are excluded; all temporary buffers and call stacks are included.
constraints: Use worst-case bounds. Count all working memory including any stack; exclude supplied inputs and the scalar result.

options.text: O(min(n*q, n log n + q log n)) time, O(n) in the worst case over inputs and q auxiliary space
O(min(n*q, n log n + q log n)) time, O(n log n) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Compare total scan cost against sort-once plus q binary searches.
details: Scanning all queries costs O(n*q). Copying/sorting once plus searching costs O(n log n+q log n). The adaptive method chooses the smaller total. Its worst-case auxiliary bound is O(n) because some workloads choose the sorted copied buffer; the scanning branch itself uses constant space.

“O(min(n*q, n log n + q log n)) time, O(n) in the worst case over inputs and q auxiliary space”: Preprocessing is worthwhile only when enough future queries repay its cost; immutable input makes the sorted copy an explicit space cost.

“O(min(n*q, n log n + q log n)) time, O(n log n) auxiliary space”: The sorted branch retains a copied buffer and bounded linear sort workspace, not n log n simultaneously stored records; the scan branch uses even less.
“O(1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Both scan and sorted-query branches have input-dependent work; choosing the cheaper one does not make reading/searching all queries constant.
